source.version: Undated working paper; the document prints no date, version, or venue. PDF metadata give a creation date of 2024-09-07 (Microsoft Word export), and the reference list cites 2024 work. The title on the document ('Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation') differs from the search-record title ('Ideas Are Dimes a Dozen'); the search record's DOI is SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.4526071. The document itself does not mention the earlier title.
source.title_on_document: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation

paper_design_summary: The paper compares three pools of new-product ideas for college students priced at $50 or less: 200 ideas sampled from ideas written by students in a 2021 product design course (before LLMs), 100 ideas generated by GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) with zero-shot prompting, and 100 generated by GPT-4 with few-shot prompting. College-age US raters on Prolific scored each idea for purchase intent (quality) and novelty, and the authors computed pairwise embedding similarity and overlap within each pool. No person received AI assistance: the design compares AI-generated output with human-generated output.

studies.label: Studies 1-3: one dataset of 400 ideas (200 student, 100 GPT-4 zero-shot, 100 GPT-4 few-shot)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned to AI. The pools differ by source (students before LLMs vs. GPT-4). The 200 student ideas were randomly selected from the course's idea pool, and ideas were shown to raters in random order, randomized at the idea level.
assignment.quote: We presented ideas in random order and randomized at the idea level, meaning that every survey participant could potentially see ideas from multiple sources.
assignment.locator: p. 12, Section 5 (rating design); p. 10, Section 4 (random selection of 200 student ideas)

arms.name: Student ideas
arms.description: 200 ideas randomly selected from ideas written in 2021 by students in a product design and innovation course at an elite university, before LLMs were available. Average description 63 words.

arms.name: GPT-4 zero-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 (temperature 0.7) from the same prompt given to students, ten at a time, with summaries of earlier ideas fed back to avoid repeats. Average 69 words.

arms.name: GPT-4 few-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 with the same prompt plus six highly rated ideas from a separate student set as examples. Average 71 words.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The unit compared is the idea: 200 student ideas, 100 zero-shot, 100 few-shot. The paper does not say how many students wrote the 200 sampled ideas.
participants.who: Idea producers: 50 students in a 2021 product design and innovation course at an unnamed elite university (no AI). Raters: college-age individuals from the United States recruited on Prolific; 200 respondents in the purchase-intent model (7,982 ratings) and 201 in the novelty model (8,023 ratings). Each respondent rated about 40 ideas; each idea was rated about 20 times.
participants.country: United States (raters); the university is not named
participants.quote: In this course, 50 students participated in an innovation challenge to come up with ideas for a physical product marketed to college students for $50 or less
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 4 (students); p. 12, Section 5 (raters); p. 31, Appendix B (N RespondentID 200, N IdeaID 400); p. 34, Appendix B Novelty (N RespondentID 201)

ai_tool.how_used: The model generated ideas on its own from the authors' prompts (zero-shot, or few-shot with six example student ideas). No human participant used the AI; the AI output is compared with pre-LLM human output.

task.description: Generate ideas for a physical product targeted at US college students and sold for about $50 or less, each expressed as a title plus a paragraph (the GPT-4 prompt asked for 40-80 words).
task.duration: Not stated for students (an innovation challenge in a one-semester course). For GPT-4, the paper says 200 ideas can be generated by one human with GPT-4 in about 15 minutes (p. 26), as a general statement.

outcomes.name: Purchase intent (idea quality)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five-box purchase-intent scale weighted 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 (Jamieson and Bass 1989), rated by Prolific college-age US respondents. Main analysis: linear mixed-effects model with source fixed effects (humans baseline) and random intercepts and slopes for respondents and ideas (7,982 ratings, 200 respondents, 400 ideas). Robustness (Section 8.2.1, pp. 23-24; Appendix B): alternative weights 0.4/0.2/0 (Ulrich and Eppinger), simple regression on idea-level means (n = 400; zero-shot +0.256, 95% CI [0.15, 0.37]; few-shot +0.358, 95% CI [0.25, 0.47], on the unweighted 0-4 scale per Appendix B intercept 1.62), cumulative link mixed model (zero-shot 0.395, few-shot 0.581), ordered logit odds ratios 1.48 and 1.79.

contrasts.reported: Mean purchase intent 46.4% (zero-shot) vs 40.4% (humans); LMM beta = 0.059; 95% CI [0.031, 0.088]; t(246) = 4.06, p < 0.001
contrasts.locator: p. 13 (means, text below Figure 1); p. 14, Section 5 (LMM); p. 30, Appendix B Purchase Intent table

contrasts.reported: Mean purchase intent 49.3% (few-shot) vs 40.4% (humans); LMM beta = 0.089; 95% CI [0.060, 0.12]; t(223) = 5.93, p < 0.001
contrasts.locator: p. 13 (means); p. 14, Section 5 (LMM); p. 30, Appendix B Purchase Intent table

contrasts.reported: AI-vs-AI prompting contrast, no humans: beta = 0.03; 95% CI [-0.01, 0.06]; t(199) = 1.892, p = 0.06 ('weakly significantly different')
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Section 5; p. 32, Appendix B 'Purchase Intent (no weights, zero-shot baseline)' (Few-Shot 0.12, CI -0.00 to 0.24, p = 0.058, unweighted scale)

outcomes.name: Quality of the best ideas (top-decile share and quantile regression of purchase intent)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas ranked by mean purchase intent across the pooled 400 ideas. Top 10% (40 ideas): share from each source and mean quality of each source's top decile (Table 3). Chi-square test of equal representation. Quantile regression of idea-level mean rating on a GPT-4 dummy (zero-shot and few-shot pooled) at quantiles 0.1-0.9 (Figure 4, Table A.1). Robustness: top 5% and top 15% (Table 4, p. 25).

contrasts.treatment_arm: GPT-4 zero-shot and few-shot (pooled and separately)
contrasts.reported: Share of top decile: Student 5/40, zero-shot 15/40, few-shot 20/40 (35 of 40, 87.5%, from GPT-4); average quality of top decile 0.62 / 0.64 / 0.66; chi-square vs equal representation (20, 10, 10): x2 = 26.39, p < 0.001, df = 2. Quantile regression at 0.9: Source AI = 0.318235*, CI [0.190531, 0.445939] (* p < 0.1%). Top 5%: 1/20, 6/20, 14/20; top 15%: 11/60, 22/60, 27/60.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 and text above it; p. 21, Figure 4; p. 30, Appendix A Table A.1; p. 25, Table 4

outcomes.name: Average pairwise cosine similarity within each pool
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings of each pair of ideas within a pool, averaged over the pool (Table 1). Higher similarity means less diverse, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity and direction below is coded on diversity. Robustness: mean edge length of a minimum spanning tree over the 512-dimensional embeddings (0 = not diverse, 1 = very diverse): Student 0.53, zero-shot 0.33, few-shot 0.3 (p. 24).

contrasts.reported: Average cosine similarity 0.415 (zero-shot) vs 0.221 (students); higher similarity = lower diversity. Three-group one-way ANOVA: eta2 = 0.455, 95% CI [-0.210, -0.204], F(2, 29598) = 12340.95, p < 0.001
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text below; p. 16, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Average cosine similarity 0.428 (few-shot) vs 0.221 (students); higher similarity = lower diversity. Same three-group ANOVA as above.
Human ideas have significantly smaller cosine similarity than GPT-4 ideas: eta2 = 0.358, 95% CI [-0.197, -0.190], F(1, 24649) = 13715.82, p < 0.001
AI-vs-AI prompting contrast: zero-shot ideas have significantly smaller cosine similarity than few-shot (0.415 vs 0.428): eta2 = 0.004, 95% CI [-0.018, -0.010], F(1, 9898) = 44.24, p < 0.001

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of idea embeddings within a pool
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each pool (200 student, 100 zero-shot, 100 few-shot)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way ANOVA treating pairwise similarities as observations (F-tests with pair-level degrees of freedom); CIs printed beside eta-squared
diversity_detail.notes: Student ideas come from up to 50 different people; each GPT-4 pool comes from one model, so this is not a comparison of people working with and without AI. The printed ANOVA degrees of freedom (29598; 24649) do not match the number of pairs implied by pool sizes; not recomputed here.

outcomes.name: Fraction of overlapping ideas (cosine similarity > 0.8)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: An idea counts as overlapping if its USE cosine similarity with an earlier idea in the pool exceeds 0.8 (text, pp. 8, 14); Table 1 notes instead define the fraction using an idea's average pairwise similarity exceeding 0.8. Robustness thresholds (p. 24): 0.7 gives 25 (zero-shot) and 37 (few-shot) overlapping ideas; 0.75 gives 16 and 23; 0.85 gives 2 and 1. Direction coded on diversity (more overlap = less diverse).

contrasts.reported: Fraction overlapping 0.05 (zero-shot) vs 0 (students; 95% CI for fraction [0.0, 0.0184]); binomial test RD = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.007], p < 0.001
Fraction overlapping 0.07 (few-shot) vs 0 (students); RD = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.120, -0.020], p < 0.001
AI-vs-AI prompting contrast: RD = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.086, 0.046], p = 0.56

diversity_detail.metric: Share of ideas in a pool whose cosine similarity with another idea exceeds 0.8
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each new idea against all previously added ideas in its pool (text); Table 1 notes describe each idea's average pairwise similarity to all other ideas in the pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Binomial test on the fraction of ideas; risk differences with 95% CIs
diversity_detail.notes: Definition differs between the text and the Table 1 notes.

outcomes.name: Estimated number of discoverable ideas (capture-recapture)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Kornish and Ulrich (2011) capture-recapture model, u(n) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-an)), T = 1/a, using overlap at the 0.8 cosine threshold. Direction coded on diversity.

contrasts.reported: 5 of 100 zero-shot and 7 of 100 few-shot ideas overlapping; u(100) = 0.95 and 0.93; estimated T = 966 ideas (zero-shot) and 680 ideas (few-shot). Human-generated ideas were all unique (estimate described as 'infinitely large', p. 15).

diversity_detail.metric: Estimated size of the opportunity space T from the rate of overlapping ideas
diversity_detail.computed_over: Sequence of ideas within each pool, each against earlier ideas
diversity_detail.notes: No interval or test reported for T.

outcomes.name: Perceived novelty
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Prolific raters answered 'Relative to other products you have seen, how novel do you consider the idea for this new product?' on 0 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 / 1 (not at all to extremely novel). Linear mixed-effects model with source fixed effects and random intercepts and slopes for respondents and ideas (8,023 ratings, 201 respondents, 400 ideas). Robustness (pp. 24-25, Appendix B): simple regression on idea means (zero-shot -0.177, 95% CI [-0.286, -0.069]; few-shot -0.197, 95% CI [-0.305, -0.089]; unweighted scale), CLMM (zero-shot -0.306, few-shot -0.39), ordered logit odds ratios 0.74 and 0.68. Top-decile average novelty 0.45 / 0.35 / 0.33 (Table 3).

contrasts.locator: p. 17, Section 6.3 (means, SDs); p. 18 (LMM) and Figure 3; p. 33, Appendix B Novelty table
p. 17, Section 6.3; p. 18 and Figure 3; p. 33, Appendix B Novelty table

contrasts.reported: AI-vs-AI prompting contrast: beta = -0.01; 95% CI [-0.039, 0.017]; t(195) = -0.757, p = 0.45

company_involvement.description: All authors list university affiliations (Wharton, Cornell). Funding from the Mack Institute for Innovation Management at Wharton. OpenAI's GPT-4 is the model studied; no company role in the research is stated.

eligibility.reason: No person was assigned to or used AI: GPT-4 generated two pools of ideas on its own, and these are compared with ideas students wrote in 2021 before LLMs (pp. 10-12). Criterion 2 fails because no participants worked under AI and no-AI conditions; the 50 student ideators and the 200/201 Prolific raters are not arms of an AI-assistance experiment. Outcomes (rated purchase intent and novelty, embedding similarity) are scored on the ideas, so criterion 3 is met in kind. Context: AI versus human output.

one_line_finding: Across 400 product ideas, GPT-4 ideas had higher mean rated purchase intent than student ideas (zero-shot 46.4 percent, few-shot 49.3 percent vs 40.4 percent; p. 13-14), lower rated novelty (36.7 and 36.1 vs 40.6 percent; p. 17-18), and higher average pairwise cosine similarity (0.415 and 0.428 vs 0.221; Table 1, p. 15).
open_questions: Figure 1 (p. 13, 'Purchase Intent by Idea Type') prints Mean 0.41 / 0.366 / 0.361 and Std 0.117 / 0.101 / 0.111, which equal the novelty statistics in Figure 3 and Section 6.3, not the purchase-intent means in the text (40.4 / 46.4 / 49.3 percent). The text says the SDs of quality are 'comparable' but gives no purchase-intent SDs elsewhere.
The introduction (p. 3) reports average purchase intent 0.48 for AI vs 0.40 for humans and novelty 0.36 vs 0.41; Section 5 gives 46.4 and 49.3 percent for the two GPT-4 pools.
Table 1 notes define the overlap fraction by an idea's average pairwise similarity exceeding 0.8, while the text defines overlap as similarity above 0.8 with any earlier idea.
How many of the 50 students wrote the 200 sampled ideas is not stated; Section 4 also refers to 'these challenges' in the plural.
notes: Treated as one study because the paper's Studies 1, 2, and 3 are analyses of the same 400-idea dataset rated by the same Prolific sample. Arm counts are ideas (200 / 100 / 100), so people counts are null. 'ai_available_when_produced' is 'mixed' because the student pool was written without AI and the GPT-4 pools were produced by the model itself, with no human user. Few-shot vs zero-shot contrasts are coded 'other' because both arms are model output with no human participants. Number of rated observations: purchase intent 7,982 (200 respondents), novelty 8,023 (201 respondents), Appendix B pp. 30-34. Ratings were collected in May and June 2023 (p. 23); IRB Penn protocol #853634 (p. 12). Not listed as outcomes: novelty-purchase intent correlation (-0.08, p. 18) and the descriptive Table 2 of top-40 ideas.
